guides.title: Betazed
guides.summary: Betazed, the Federation member world and homeworld of the telepathic Betazoid people — the planet's culture and customs, its noble houses, notable Betazoids, and the Dominion occupation of Betazed during the war.

sections.heading: The World
sections.body:
Betazed is a class M world and Federation member, homeworld of the Betazoid species. It is widely accounted one of the most beautiful planets in the Federation: temperate, green, rich in lakes and formal gardens, with cities built to be walked through rather than defended. The planet has long been a favoured site for diplomatic conferences, artistic gatherings and honeymoons — a reputation its inhabitants cultivate without embarrassment.

Its people are outwardly indistinguishable from Humans except for uniformly dark irises, and its society is prosperous, peaceful and old; Betazed's recorded civilization predates its Federation membership by many centuries. Records differ on the precise date of admission, but by the mid-24th century Betazed stood among the Federation's established core worlds, contributing diplomats, counsellors and scientists in numbers far out of proportion to its population. The planet's defining fact, from which nearly everything else about it follows, is that its natives are telepaths.

sections.heading: Telepathy and the Betazoid Mind
sections.body:
Betazoids are natural telepaths. Among themselves, full telepathic conversation is ordinary — many Betazoids on their homeworld speak aloud chiefly for the benefit of visitors — and with most other species they read surface thoughts and emotional states with ease. The ability normally develops in adolescence, arriving gradually as the mind learns to filter. The rare Betazoid born with telepathy fully active suffers for it: unable to screen out the thoughts of others, such individuals often struggle severely, and some, like the noted contact specialist Tam Elbrun, find peace only in unusual assignments.

The ability has limits. Betazoids cannot read certain species — Ferengi, Breen and Dopterians among them, owing to their neuroanatomy — and artificial minds are opaque to them. Children of Betazoid and other-species parentage are typically empathic rather than fully telepathic, sensing emotion but not thought, as with the half-Betazoid Starfleet counsellor Deanna Troi. Betazoid ethics treat the deliberate deep reading of an unwilling mind as a serious violation, and Betazoid law and custom enforce that restraint far more firmly than outsiders tend to assume.

sections.heading: Culture and Customs
sections.body:
A society of telepaths keeps few secrets, and Betazoid culture is built around that fact. Candour is the cardinal virtue; polite evasion, so useful elsewhere, is regarded on Betazed as both futile and faintly insulting. Emotional openness is taught as a discipline rather than an indulgence, and Betazoid art, therapy and jurisprudence all assume that what a person feels can, in principle, be known.

Tradition runs deep. Betazoid society preserves aristocratic houses — Ambassador Lwaxana Troi famously styled herself a daughter of the Fifth House, holder of the Sacred Chalice of Rixx and heir to the Holy Rings of Betazed — though the modern weight of such titles is social rather than political. Ceremony is elaborate: gifts at a Betazoid wedding follow precise custom, and the wedding itself is traditionally conducted with all participants unclothed, a practice signifying that nothing is concealed between the joining families. The word imzadi, often rendered simply as beloved, carries particular weight, denoting the first person to touch one's heart and mind together; Betazoids regard the bond it names as unrepeatable.

sections.heading: The Dominion Occupation
sections.body:
In 2374, during the Dominion War, Betazed fell. A Dominion assault force struck while the Tenth Fleet, assigned to the sector's defence, was out of position on a training exercise, and the planet's own defences — outdated and lightly manned after generations of peace — were overwhelmed in a matter of hours. The loss shocked the Federation as few defeats did: a core member world, famous for gentleness, was under Jem'Hadar garrison, and the Dominion was suddenly positioned to threaten Vulcan, Andor, Tellar and the approaches to Earth itself.

Occupation sat strangely on a world of telepaths. Accounts from the period describe quiet, organized resistance, the population's abilities making concealment from collaborators nearly impossible and concealment from the occupiers surprisingly practical. Betazed was restored to Federation control before the war's end; records of the liberation itself are sparser than the event deserves, and histories differ on details. The occupation left lasting marks — memorials stand in several cities — and it permanently ended the old Betazoid habit of treating defence as somebody else's profession.

sections.heading: Notable Betazoids
sections.body:
Betazed's contribution to Federation life runs strongly through diplomacy and the counselling disciplines, where telepathy and empathy are professional instruments. Ambassador Lwaxana Troi served for decades as one of the Federation's most conspicuous envoys, her flamboyance concealing genuine skill; her daughter, Commander Deanna Troi, half Betazoid and half Human, served as ship's counsellor aboard the Enterprise-D and Enterprise-E and stood in the first rank of her profession. Tam Elbrun, born with his telepathy fully active, became a specialist in contact with non-humanoid intelligences, most famously the living ship known as Tin Man.

Not every notable Betazoid fits the pattern. Lon Suder, a Betazoid crewman aboard the starship Voyager, was born without measurable empathy — a rarity among his species — and his violent life and redemptive death are studied in both psychiatric and ethical literature. Betazoids serve throughout Starfleet and the diplomatic corps, though the temptation to rely on them for interrogation has been periodically controversial — precisely because Betazoid ethics restrain what Betazoid ability could do.

guides.title: Trill, the Planet
guides.summary: Trill, homeworld of the Trill species and the symbionts: the Caves of Mak'ala, the Symbiosis Commission, the joining of hosts and symbionts, and how joined Trill shape the planet's society and its place in the Federation.

sections.heading: The World
sections.body:
Trill is a class M world, a Federation member, and the homeworld of two sentient species living in the closest partnership known to Federation science: the humanoid Trill and the vermiform symbionts. The planet itself is temperate and pleasant, noted for its seas and for the geothermal cave systems that make its deep interior habitable to symbionts. Trill cities blend a very old architectural tradition with unremarkable modern prosperity; a visitor could spend weeks on the surface without seeing anything to suggest the planet's extraordinary biology.

Humanoid Trill are distinguished by twin rows of dappled spots running from the temples down the sides of the body. The great majority of Trill are unjoined and live ordinary single lives; the joined — those carrying a symbiont — are a small, honoured minority around whom much of the society's high culture, most of its institutions of consequence, and nearly all of its mystery are organized.

sections.heading: Hosts and Symbionts
sections.body:
The symbionts are long-lived, sightless, vermiform beings who cannot survive on the surface unassisted. Placed within a humanoid Trill host through a surgical joining, symbiont and host become a single blended person: the host's body and voice, the symbiont's centuries of accumulated memory, and a personality that is genuinely neither and both. When a host dies, the symbiont is transferred to a new host and the blend forms again; a symbiont may live through eight or ten hosts, and a newly joined Trill wakes with lifetimes of memory that are suddenly their own.

The joining is union rather than possession — each successive host contributes permanently to the symbiont's continuity — and Trill custom marks it by name: a joined Trill takes the symbiont's name as a surname, so that Curzon Dax, Jadzia Dax and Ezri Dax are three people and, in a sense Trill do not find paradoxical, one lineage. After roughly ninety-three hours the bond becomes physiologically permanent; removing the symbiont thereafter kills the host, and a symbiont left unjoined too long dies as well.

sections.heading: The Caves of Mak'ala
sections.body:
Unjoined symbionts live in the Caves of Mak'ala, a deep network of interconnected pools of nutrient-rich, milky water warmed by the planet's interior. There the symbionts are spawned, mature over decades, and pass the portions of their lives between hosts. They communicate with one another through patterned electrical discharges that flicker visibly through the pools — a language no humanoid has fully rendered.

The pools are tended by the Guardians, an order of unjoined Trill who devote their lives to the symbionts' care and who, by long immersion in that duty, develop an uncanny sensitivity to the beings they serve; Guardians have been known to recognize a returning symbiont through an unfamiliar new host at a glance. Joined Trill occasionally return to Mak'ala to immerse themselves and commune directly with the unjoined, and symbionts in medical distress are brought back to the pools when nothing else will serve. The caves are the closest thing Trill civilization has to sacred ground, access is closely restricted, and most Trill live and die without ever seeing them.

sections.heading: The Symbiosis Commission and the Truth About Joining
sections.body:
Joining is administered by the Symbiosis Commission, the planet's most powerful institution. Candidates — initiates — compete through years of academic, psychological and ethical evaluation, supervised in the field by joined mentors called docents whose recommendation can end a candidacy; only a fraction of applicants are ever matched with a symbiont. The Commission's public doctrine long held that perhaps one Trill in a thousand could survive a joining, making rigorous selection a medical necessity.

That doctrine is false, and the Commission knows it. Investigation in 2371, following a medical crisis of the Dax symbiont, established that roughly half the Trill population is biologically capable of joining. The figure is suppressed because symbionts are few and would-be hosts are many; were the truth generally known, the Commission fears, symbionts would become commodities to be bought, stolen and fought over. Records differ on how widely the fact has since spread — it has certainly surfaced in Starfleet medical channels — but the official fiction stands, and it remains the sharpest ethical controversy in an otherwise transparent society.

sections.heading: Law, Ritual and the Federation
sections.body:
Trill custom binds the joined with rules the unjoined never face. The gravest is the taboo against reassociation: successive hosts may not resume the romantic attachments of a predecessor's life, on the principle that each host must live a life of its own rather than continue another's. The penalty is exile from future joining — death, in effect, for the symbiont's line — and the taboo has been tested publicly at least once, when Jadzia Dax was reunited with the wife of a former host. Ritual balances law: in the zhian'tara, a joined Trill's past hosts are each temporarily embodied in the minds of volunteering friends, letting the present host meet, argue with and take proper leave of the people they contain.

Within the Federation, Trill serve everywhere, and the Dax lineage alone illustrates the reach: Curzon Dax a celebrated diplomat and negotiator with the Klingon Empire, Jadzia Dax a decorated Starfleet science officer of the Dominion War, Ezri Dax a counsellor joined under emergency conditions. Joined officers are prized for the depth of lived experience they carry — and watched, quietly, for the weight of it.

guides.title: Memory Alpha, the Federation Archive
guides.summary: Memory Alpha, the planetoid housing the Federation's central library and archive — its open-access charter, the memory core, the 2269 Zetarian attack that destroyed the archive's heart, and its place in Federation scholarship.

sections.heading: Charter and Purpose
sections.body:
Memory Alpha is a planetoid set aside by the United Federation of Planets as its central library: a single site assembling the cultural history and scientific knowledge of every Federation member. Its charter is deliberately universalist — the archive exists for all scholars, of any world, and its holdings are open rather than classified. In its original conception that openness was physical as well as legal: the facility was built without defensive shielding, on the stated principle that a library of the galaxy's knowledge should stand as an academy, not a fortress.

The planetoid itself is small, airless on the surface, and given over entirely to the archive's purposes: data storage complexes, research habitats, laboratories and residence sections for a resident population of scholars and technicians drawn from across the Federation. For researchers, a posting to Memory Alpha has long carried the prestige that a great university chair carries on a member world; for starship crews, it is a standard port of call for depositing survey records and drawing reference data.

sections.heading: The Memory Core
sections.body:
The heart of the facility is the memory core, the computer complex holding the archive itself. In the late 2260s the core underwent a major consolidation, drawing the accumulated records of the member worlds into a newly assembled central complex — an undertaking that concentrated, for a time, an irreplaceable fraction of Federation knowledge in one place. The core's indexing and retrieval systems were counted among the finest information engineering of the era, capable of serving thousands of simultaneous research queries across the archive's full breadth.

That concentration was the design's strength and its flaw. Duplication of the newest acquisitions to member-world archives lagged behind the consolidation, and the facility's founding refusal of shields meant the core's protection rested on Memory Alpha's obscurity and on the assumption that no one attacks a library. The assumption failed within a few years of the consolidation, and the archive's later history is largely the working-out of that lesson.

sections.heading: The Zetarian Attack of 2269
sections.body:
In 2269 Memory Alpha was attacked by a phenomenon initially logged as an energy storm: in fact a community of noncorporeal survivors of the dead world Zetar, seeking living minds through which to continue their existence. Passing through the unshielded facility, the entities killed the resident staff — the archive's scholars and technicians died at their stations — and burned out the newly assembled memory core, destroying its contents beyond recovery. The starship Enterprise, arriving with a technical team, could do no more than confirm the losses and pursue the phenomenon, which was finally neutralized after it attempted to claim one of the ship's own officers.

The material cost was severe: whatever had not yet been duplicated to member-world archives was gone outright, and contemporary assessments called the loss to Federation scholarship irreparable. The human cost ended the innocence of the founding charter. No serious voice proposed abandoning the open-archive principle, but the belief that openness required defencelessness did not survive the year.

sections.heading: Reconstruction and Hardening
sections.body:
Memory Alpha was rebuilt. The archive was restocked from member-world holdings, starship libraries and private collections — a salvage of scholarship that took years and remained, by honest accounting, incomplete — and the facility resumed operations under a revised doctrine. The core lesson was distribution: no single consolidation of unduplicated records was permitted again, and the archive's later architecture kept synchronized copies flowing outward to member worlds as fast as acquisitions flowed in. Later records refer to sister facilities in the same tradition, suggesting the Federation ultimately answered the risk with redundancy rather than armour; accounts differ on how that network was organized, and on what defensive measures the rebuilt planetoid itself finally accepted.

What is certain is that the attack changed archival practice across the Federation. Starship record-keeping standards, the routine deposit of duplicate logs, and the reflexive mirroring of scientific data all trace, in part, to 2269 — a catastrophe remembered less for what was lost than for what it taught.

sections.heading: The Archive in Federation Life
sections.body:
Memory Alpha's name became shorthand for the Federation's institutional memory. Starships synchronize their library computers against its holdings when in range; survey commands deposit raw findings there as a condition of publication; and historians, jurists and xenologists treat its collections as the reference of record when accounts conflict. Its cataloguing conventions spread outward with its data, so that a researcher trained on one member world can navigate another's archives without translation.

The facility also serves quieter functions. It arbitrates: when member worlds' histories disagree, Memory Alpha's practice is to preserve the disagreement rather than resolve it, holding rival accounts side by side with their provenance attached. It remembers the small as well as the great — folk music, minor patents, village records — on the charter principle that a civilization's knowledge is not only its masterpieces. And it stands as a symbol: a working demonstration that a hundred worlds' memory can be held in common, which is, in miniature, the Federation's own claim about itself.

guides.title: Jupiter Station
guides.summary: Jupiter Station, the Starfleet research and operations complex orbiting Jupiter in the Sol system — home of the Holoprogramming Center where Doctor Lewis Zimmerman developed the Emergency Medical Hologram.

sections.heading: Overview and Location
sections.body:
Jupiter Station is a Starfleet installation in orbit of Jupiter, in the Sol system. It is one of the oldest continuously operated orbital facilities in the Federation's home system, serving over its long life as a research complex, an operations and support post, and a waypoint in the busy traffic between Earth, the Utopia Planitia Fleet Yards at Mars, and the outer system. Records differ on the station's original commissioning, and its structure has been enlarged and rebuilt so many times that little of any first configuration can remain.

The station's modern reputation rests on research. Its laboratory divisions have hosted work across holography, cybernetics, medicine and starship systems, and its position — deep inside the best-defended star system in the Federation, yet away from Earth's crowded orbitals — has made it a natural home for programmes that want both security and room to work. To most Starfleet personnel, however, Jupiter Station means one thing above all: the birthplace of the Emergency Medical Hologram.

sections.heading: Structure and Operations
sections.body:
Accounts describe Jupiter Station as a complex of stacked and linked modules — paired saucer sections on connecting spines are the configuration most often depicted — supporting laboratories, habitat sections, docking facilities and communications arrays. The station maintains standard Starfleet operations functions: it supports traffic control and logistics for the Jovian region, services small craft, and provides a duty posting for scientific and engineering personnel who rotate between the station, Earth and the Mars yards.

Daily life aboard is by all accounts closer to a research campus than a frontier outpost. The station's population mixes Starfleet officers with civilian specialists, and its laboratory culture has historically tolerated the eccentric — a tolerance tested, by well-attested account, by some of its most distinguished residents. Jupiter's radiation environment and the traffic of the home system keep the operations staff genuinely busy, but the station has rarely seen combat, and its history is written mainly in publications and patents rather than battle honours.

sections.heading: The Holoprogramming Center
sections.body:
Jupiter Station's most celebrated division is its holoprogramming centre, the Starfleet facility for advanced holographic research, directed for many years by Doctor Lewis Zimmerman — widely regarded as the father of modern medical holography. It was here in the early 2370s that Zimmerman created the Emergency Medical Hologram: a fully interactive holographic physician, carrying the accumulated knowledge of thousands of medical references, designed to activate when a ship's medical staff was dead, disabled or overwhelmed. Zimmerman modelled the EMH Mark I's appearance and, less deliberately, its temperament on himself — a decision with consequences he spent years living down.

The Mark I's abrasive bedside manner led to its replacement by successive marks and, notoriously, to the recall and reassignment of many Mark I programs to menial labour; accounts describe them scrubbing plasma conduits aboard waste transfer barges, a fate that later became a point of debate about the standing of sentient-seeming programs. The centre's work continued through later EMH generations and related projects, including an attempted Long-term Medical Hologram, and its research underpins much of the Federation's subsequent holographic practice.

sections.heading: The EMH Legacy and the 2377 Incident
sections.body:
The holoprogramming centre's most famous product proved itself far from home. The EMH aboard the starship Voyager — a Mark I — ran continuously for years after that ship was stranded in the Delta Quadrant, vastly beyond design life, and grew far past his programming, adding surgical innovations, command training, friendships and creative pursuits no specification anticipated.

In 2377, word reached Voyager that Doctor Zimmerman was dying of a degenerative condition Federation medicine had failed to arrest. Voyager's EMH had himself transmitted across the intervening light-years to Jupiter Station by way of a newly established data link — at the time among the longest transfers of a sentient program ever attempted — and, after a difficult reunion in which creator and creation found each other equally impossible, treated Zimmerman successfully with medical techniques acquired in the Delta Quadrant. The episode is remembered at the station both as a medical footnote and as a milestone in the question of holographic personhood: the program built to be a stopgap had returned home as, by any practical measure, a colleague.

sections.heading: Notable Personnel
sections.body:
Doctor Lewis Zimmerman dominates the station's roll of names: brilliant, vain, solitary, and by most accounts happiest in the company of the holograms he built — including Haley, a long-serving holographic assistant whom he treated, on his own inconsistent account, as something between a colleague and family. Lieutenant Reginald Barclay of Starfleet's Pathfinder Project, himself a noted holographic-systems engineer, worked closely with Zimmerman during the 2377 incident and afterward; Counsellor Deanna Troi of the Enterprise also attended, summoned to mediate between the dying designer and the physician he refused to be treated by.

Beyond the holography programme, the station's laboratories have hosted researchers whose names survive mainly in the technical literature, which is how Jupiter Station prefers it. Its contribution to Starfleet is measured in systems quietly working aboard every ship of the line — and in one physician, copied and recopied across the fleet, who began as a subroutine in a Jovian laboratory.

guides.title: The Bajoran Wormhole
guides.summary: The stable wormhole in the Bajoran system linking the Alpha and Gamma Quadrants, known to Bajor as the Celestial Temple of the Prophets. Covers the wormhole's discovery near station Deep Space 9, the wormhole aliens and the Orbs, and its role in the Dominion War.

sections.heading: Discovery and Location
sections.body:
The Bajoran wormhole is the only stable wormhole known to Federation science. Its Alpha Quadrant terminus sits in the Denorios Belt, a charged plasma field in the Bajoran system, and its far mouth opens in the Gamma Quadrant near the Idran system, roughly seventy thousand light-years away. A vessel can make the crossing in minutes; the same journey at high warp would consume the better part of a lifetime.

The wormhole was charted in 2369 by Commander Benjamin Sisko and Lieutenant Jadzia Dax of station Deep Space 9, shortly after the Cardassian withdrawal from Bajor. Its discovery transformed a war-scarred frontier world into one of the most strategically significant systems in the quadrant, and the station was moved from Bajoran orbit to the wormhole's mouth to secure and administer it.

Bajoran records suggest the wormhole had made itself known long before Starfleet arrived. Orbs — artifacts of the beings within — had appeared over Bajor across ten thousand years, and Bajoran faith had long held that the Celestial Temple of the Prophets lay hidden in the heavens near the Denorios Belt.

sections.heading: Structure and Stability
sections.body:
Unlike naturally occurring wormholes, which decay within hours or shift their termini unpredictably, the Bajoran wormhole is fixed at both ends and has remained open across every recorded transit. Analysis attributes this stability to verteron nodes within the passage: self-sustaining structures that hold the corridor open and permit conventional vessels to pass without engaging warp drive inside.

The interior does not behave as normal space. Sensor logs from thousands of transits describe a luminous corridor with measurable thresholds at either terminus, yet time and distance inside do not always correspond to external readings. Some crews report the passage as nearly instantaneous; others record several minutes of transit.

The wormhole is not indestructible, and it can be sealed or altered. In 2374 it was closed briefly when a pah-wraith entered the passage, and it has been reduced to intermittent subspace visibility more than once by external interference. On each occasion it was restored. Standing Starfleet guidance treats the wormhole as an artificial construct maintained by its inhabitants rather than a natural phenomenon, and cautions that its continued operation ultimately depends on them.

sections.heading: The Prophets and the Celestial Temple
sections.body:
The wormhole is inhabited. The beings within — called the Prophets by the Bajoran faith and identified in Starfleet records as the wormhole aliens — exist outside linear time. They do not experience past, present, and future in sequence, and early contact required Commander Sisko to explain the concept of linear existence itself.

To Bajor, the wormhole is the Celestial Temple, the dwelling of the Prophets who have guided Bajoran civilization for millennia. The Orbs, hourglass-shaped energy artifacts that induce visions in those who encounter them, are regarded as gifts of the Prophets, and several are held in Bajoran keeping.

The Prophets have intervened directly in physical events on at least one occasion. In late 2373, as a Dominion fleet of thousands of ships crossed the wormhole toward the Alpha Quadrant, the fleet vanished within the passage and never emerged. Records attribute this to the Prophets acting at the request of Benjamin Sisko, whom Bajoran faith names the Emissary — a role that came to bind Federation, Bajoran, and religious history together in a single officer.

sections.heading: Strategic Value and the Dominion War
sections.body:
As the only reliable passage between the Alpha and Gamma Quadrants, the wormhole reshaped politics on both sides of the galaxy. Commerce, exploration, and colonization traffic flowed through it within months of discovery, and first contact with the Dominion — the dominant power of the Gamma Quadrant — followed in 2370.

When war came, the wormhole was its center of gravity. Dominion reinforcements could reach Cardassian space only through the passage, and control of Deep Space 9 meant control of the door. In 2373 Starfleet mined the wormhole's mouth with self-replicating cloaked mines rather than allow further Jem'Hadar convoys through, a decision that opened the general war. The station fell, the minefield held for months, and its eventual destruction in 2374 was answered by Operation Return, the fleet action that retook the station.

Records differ on how close the Alpha Quadrant came to defeat in those months. What is not disputed is that a single stable wormhole made a remote frontier system the most contested position in known space, and that possession of it decided the shape of the war.

sections.heading: Aftermath and Continuing Significance
sections.body:
The wormhole's later history remains eventful. In 2375, at the war's end, the Emissary entered the Celestial Temple, and Bajoran teaching holds that he remains with the Prophets. The passage itself continues to operate, and traffic between the quadrants resumed under joint Bajoran and Federation administration from Deep Space 9.

Scientific interest has never faded. The wormhole remains the only laboratory in which a stable subspace corridor can be studied directly, and much of Federation wormhole theory rests on data gathered at the Denorios Belt. Attempts to replicate its stability artificially have not succeeded, and the verteron mechanics that hold it open remain only partially understood.

For Bajor, the wormhole is not infrastructure but scripture made visible, and every assessment of the region that ignores this has misread it. The faith of a civilization, the economy of two quadrants, the largest war of the century, and the only fixed bridge across the galaxy's breadth converge at a single point of light that opens and closes above the Denorios Belt — recorded by Starfleet as the Bajoran wormhole, and by Bajor as the Temple gates.

guides.title: The Delta Quadrant
guides.summary: The galactic quadrant on the far side of the core from Federation space — heartland of the Borg Collective and the region crossed by the starship USS Voyager. Covers the quadrant's extent, its powers and species, and the seven-year Voyager crossing.

sections.heading: Definition and Extent
sections.body:
Federation cartography divides the galaxy into four quadrants along two perpendicular planes crossing at the galactic core. The Delta Quadrant lies on the far side of the core from Federation space, bordering the Beta Quadrant on one side and the Gamma Quadrant on the other. At its nearest it begins tens of thousands of light-years beyond the farthest Federation outpost; the region charted by Starfleet lies roughly seventy thousand light-years from Earth.

No Federation vessel can reach the quadrant by conventional warp within a working lifetime. A crossing at sustainable cruise speeds is measured in decades — the figure most often cited is seventy-five years — which is why nearly everything Starfleet knows about the region was gathered by a single ship that did not travel there by choice.

The quadrant's scale should not be understated. It contains hundreds of billions of stars, of which Starfleet has charted only a narrow corridor. Every assessment of the Delta Quadrant is in truth an assessment of that corridor, and the quadrant beyond it remains almost entirely unknown.

sections.heading: Early Federation Contact
sections.body:
The first confirmed Federation presence in the Delta Quadrant predates any deliberate mission. In 2365 the entity known as Q transported the USS Enterprise-D some seven thousand light-years beyond Federation space to system J-25, where the crew made first contact with the Borg. Later analysis placed that encounter in or near Delta Quadrant space, and it gave Starfleet its first warning of what the quadrant contained.

Sustained contact began in 2371, when a coherent tetryon beam swept the USS Voyager from the Badlands to the far edge of the quadrant. The displacement was the work of the Caretaker, an ancient entity sustaining the Ocampa species, whose array had pulled ships across the galaxy for years. The Caretaker's death and the destruction of the array left Voyager stranded.

Fragmentary earlier contacts exist in the record. Wreckage and survivors encountered during Voyager's transit established that other Alpha Quadrant vessels had been displaced before her, and Borg activity observed in the Alpha and Beta Quadrants had Delta Quadrant origins reaching back well before the J-25 encounter.

sections.heading: Major Powers and Species
sections.body:
The charted corridor of the quadrant holds no single dominant government comparable to the Federation. Nearest the Caretaker's former array, early encounters were dominated by the Kazon — a fractious warrior culture divided into rival sects — and the Vidiians, whose civilization was being consumed by the phage and who harvested organs from other species to survive.

Further along the corridor lie the Hirogen, nomadic hunters whose entire society is organized around the pursuit of prey; the Krenim, whose mastery of temporal weaponry made them briefly capable of rewriting history; the Devore Imperium, a security state hostile to telepaths; and the Malon, whose economy exports antimatter waste into space others inhabit. The Voth, a saurian civilization of great age and power, hold to a doctrine that obscures their apparent origin on ancient Earth.

Records also preserve friendlier contacts: the Talaxians, one of whom served aboard Voyager for most of her crossing; the Ocampa, a short-lived telepathic species; and dozens of worlds that rendered aid to a ship with no allies. The picture is of a quadrant of extraordinary diversity, largely unconsolidated, and shaped at its center by a single overwhelming exception.

sections.heading: The Borg Heartland
sections.body:
That exception is the Borg Collective. The Delta Quadrant is the origin and center of Borg civilization, and vast regions of it are assimilated space. Voyager's sensors recorded thousands of cubes, unicomplexes of staggering scale, and a transwarp conduit network radiating across the galaxy, with hubs capable of delivering Borg vessels to any quadrant.

Transit through Borg space was the most dangerous passage of Voyager's journey. The ship survived it initially through a brief and unrepeatable alliance: the Collective was losing a war against Species 8472, a power from fluidic space that the Borg themselves had provoked, and Voyager traded a means of ending that war for safe passage.

Starfleet's later understanding of the Borg rests heavily on Delta Quadrant data — on the liberated drone Seven of Nine, on captured transwarp charts, and on the final engagement of Voyager's return, in which a Borg transwarp hub was destroyed from within. Assessments differ on how severely those events wounded the Collective; the record states only that the Borg remain the defining power of the quadrant.

sections.heading: The Voyager Crossing
sections.body:
USS Voyager's return journey is the axis of Federation knowledge of the quadrant. Stranded in 2371 with a projected seventy-five-year transit, the ship reached Earth in 2378, compressing the crossing to seven years through a series of exceptional means: a graviton catapult, borrowed transwarp and slipstream technologies, a stretch of empty space crossed in months, and finally a Borg transwarp corridor seized in the ship's last engagement.

The crossing was also a diplomatic mission conducted at speed. Voyager made first contact with more species in seven years than most starships record in a career, fought when cornered, and left behind treaties, enemies, and at least one continuing colony of displaced Talaxians.

From 2374 the ship was no longer wholly alone. The Pathfinder project at Starfleet Communications established intermittent contact, first through an alien relay network and later through a micro-wormhole datalink, restoring command traffic, medical consultation, and letters from home. Pathfinder marked the first time Starfleet had operated a vessel across a galactic-scale distance, and its methods remain the basis of long-range communications doctrine.

sections.heading: Assessment and Open Questions
sections.body:
Starfleet's charts of the Delta Quadrant describe a corridor, not a quadrant. The mapped region is a thread across a volume containing hundreds of billions of stars, and the great civilizations of the unexplored remainder — if they exist — are unrecorded.

Standing assessments emphasize three facts. The quadrant is the seat of the Borg Collective, and any resurgence there will eventually reach Federation space through transwarp infrastructure. It is reachable: wormholes, displacement phenomena, and captured Borg technology have all bridged the distance, and what has happened by accident can happen again in either direction. And it is not empty of friends; Voyager's logs record as many acts of aid as of hostility.

Records differ on the quadrant's future significance. Some analyses expect renewed contact within a generation, driven by slipstream research and the Pathfinder legacy; others note that every crossing to date has depended on technology the Federation does not control. Until that changes, the Delta Quadrant remains what it was in 2371 — the far side of the galaxy, known almost entirely through the log of a single ship.

guides.title: Andoria
guides.summary: Andoria is the icebound homeworld of the Andorians and a founding world of the United Federation of Planets — an ice moon of underground cities, home to the Andorian and Aenar peoples, the Imperial Guard, and customs such as the ushaan duel.

sections.heading: An Ice Moon of a Gas Giant
sections.body:
Andoria — natively Andor; both names appear throughout Federation records — is commonly described as an ice moon orbiting a ringed gas giant, though older charts list it as a planet in its own right and Andorians use the terms interchangeably. Its surface is locked in ice for most of the year, with temperatures that rise above freezing only briefly in high summer, and even then only in the equatorial belt.

Andorian civilisation accordingly went underground. The great cities are built into the crust beneath the ice, warmed by geothermal energy and connected by deep transit tunnels, with only sensor masts, ports and defensive installations breaking the surface. The largest of these buried cities serves as the capital, and Andorians speak of going up to the weather rather than out into it.

The ice itself is not lifeless. Subsurface oceans and thermal vents support native ecosystems, and Andorian cuisine and industry both draw on them heavily. Visitors are advised that the phrase mild weather in an Andorian itinerary describes conditions most humanoid species would classify as an emergency, and that their hosts consider this observation the best joke on the moon.

sections.heading: The Andorians
sections.body:
Andorians are a blue-skinned humanoid species distinguished by paired antennae rising from the crown of the head. The antennae are sensory organs, registering air movement, electromagnetic fields and subtleties of balance; they also express emotion more honestly than an Andorian face, and etiquette turns on pretending not to notice. Losing an antenna is disorienting and deeply humiliating, though it regrows within months.

Andorian physiology is adapted to cold, with an elevated metabolism that lends the species its characteristic intensity. Andorians describe themselves as a passionate people and a martial one, and their history bears this out: clan feuds and long confrontations with neighbouring powers, above all the Vulcans, fill their pre-Federation records.

That martial reputation is often misread. Andorian aggression is bounded by an elaborate code of honour, and the same culture that produced the Imperial Guard produced celebrated poets, composers and glass-artists. Andorian marriages are traditionally contracted among four partners, and family obligation is taken as seriously as any oath of service. An Andorian who names an offworlder friend is understood to have made a binding declaration, and expects it to be treated as one.

sections.heading: The Aenar
sections.body:
The Aenar are a subspecies of Andorian native to the northern wastes, distinguished by ice-white skin, blindness, and telepathy. They perceive their surroundings through the telepathic sense with such precision that sight is not missed, and their gift extends to reading and, rarely, projecting into the minds of others.

Aenar society is small — numbering in the low thousands during the twenty-second century — and rigorously pacifist. The Aenar refuse to read a mind without consent, hold leadership to be a temporary burden rather than an honour, and historically withdrew so completely from Andorian society that most Andorians regarded them as legend.

Contact was re-established in 2154, in the aftermath of an incident in which the Romulan Star Empire abducted an Aenar and used his telepathy to pilot remote drone ships against shipping across the region. The episode brought the Aenar out of isolation on their own cautious terms. Intermarriage between Andorian and Aenar lines, though rare, is recorded, and later centuries note Aenar serving offworld in scientific and diplomatic roles — never, by their own unbroken law, in combat.

sections.heading: Government and the Imperial Guard
sections.body:
The Andorian state of the pre-Federation era was the Andorian Empire, governed from the homeworld through a chancellery and the representation of the great clans; records of its internal constitution are fragmentary in Federation archives, and Andorian historians dispute how imperial the Empire ever truly was.

Its most prominent institution was the Andorian Imperial Guard, the unified military and exploratory service. The Guard was, and remains, central to Andorian identity: service conferred standing on one's clan, its officers were expected to be duellists and diplomats by turns, and its cruisers — fast, heavily armed and painted with clan honours — were respected by every power on their borders. Commander Thy'lek Shran of the warship Kumari is the Guard officer best known to Federation history, a decorated veteran of the Vulcan cold war who became, somewhat against his own instincts, an architect of interstellar peace.

After Federation membership the Guard was folded into joint defence arrangements while retaining its name, uniforms and traditions. Andoria contributes heavily to Starfleet, and Andorian officers are famously overrepresented in tactical and security postings — a statistic Andorians cite with entirely unconcealed pride.

sections.heading: The Road to the Federation
sections.body:
Andoria's path to the Federation ran through its oldest enmity. For generations the Empire and the Vulcan High Command skirmished over border worlds and surveillance posts — the disputed planetoid the Vulcans called Paan Mokar was fortified and re-fortified by both sides — and each power regarded the other as the region's principal threat.

Human mediation broke the pattern. In the 2150s Earth's Starfleet found itself repeatedly standing between the two powers: at the P'Jem monastery, where a hidden Vulcan listening post was exposed; at Weytahn, as the Andorians name Paan Mokar, where Captain Jonathan Archer and Commander Shran negotiated a workable ceasefire; and in the Babel crisis of 2154, when a Romulan campaign to set the region's powers against one another was uncovered and defeated by a joint Andorian, Vulcan, Tellarite and Human fleet.

That improvised alliance proved durable. Andoria signed the Federation Charter as one of the four founding worlds in 2161, and Andorian blue is one of the colours traditionally read into the Federation seal. The old rivalry with Vulcan survives, defanged, as athletic competition, academic polemic and a vast repertoire of in-law jokes.

sections.heading: Culture and the Ushaan
sections.body:
Andorian culture prizes honour, candour and endurance, and its most famous institution is the ushaan: a formal duel of grievance fought with the ushaan-tor, the ice-miner's blade. The code governing it runs to thousands of amendments, and its provisions for substitution, postponement and settlement mean that most declared duels end without blood — the declaration itself restores honour. Duels fought to the death were nonetheless recorded well into the twenty-second century, and the right to declare ushaan has never been formally abolished, a fact Andorian diplomats occasionally allow their counterparts to remember.

Andorian arts favour the durable and the communal: blade-craft and metalwork, choral music scored for the resonance of tunnel cities, and ice-sculpture displayed in surface galleries where it lasts exactly one season and is mourned when it goes. Andorian ale, a potent blue brew, has conquered more territory than the Imperial Guard ever did.

Cuisine is famously robust. Visitors are offered farmed tubers, vent-shrimp and the delicacy known as Andorian redbat, and are judged, gently but permanently, on their willingness to try it. Refusing food outright is rude; asking for it mild is merely funny.

guides.title: Bajor, the Planet
guides.summary: Bajor, homeworld of the Bajoran people: an ancient world of deep faith, scarred by the Cardassian occupation and transformed by the wormhole at its doorstep. Covers the planet and worlds of its system, the Prophets, the provisional government, and the road to Federation membership.

sections.heading: An Ancient World
sections.body:
Bajor is a class-M world in the Bajoran system, ringed by moons and blessed with a biosphere that Bajoran art has celebrated for as long as Bajoran art has existed, which is a very long time. By their own reckoning, Bajoran civilization is among the oldest still flourishing in the quadrant, with cultural records reaching back hundreds of millennia; Bajorans were builders and astronomers in eras when most of their later neighbors had no history at all.

Their achievements were not confined to the surface. Centuries before the warp era reached their region, Bajoran crews crossed interstellar distances in solar-sail lightships riding the tachyon eddies of their system, and Bajoran accounts hold that such vessels reached Cardassia itself, a claim long dismissed and eventually vindicated. Traditional Bajoran society was ordered by the d'jarra caste system, which assigned families to callings from artistry to soldiery; the castes were set aside in the crucible of the occupation and have not been restored. What endured instead was the faith, which has outlived every other Bajoran institution.

sections.heading: The Prophets and the Faith
sections.body:
Bajoran religion centers on the Prophets, beings the faithful hold to be the guardians and teachers of Bajor, dwelling in the Celestial Temple beyond linear time. The faith is not abstract. Over many centuries, artifacts called Orbs, the Tears of the Prophets, appeared in Bajor's skies, and encounters with them produce visions that Bajorans treat as direct communication. The Orbs are kept, studied, and venerated, and several were carried off during the occupation and later recovered piece by piece.

The church is led by the kai, chosen from the Vedek Assembly, and vedeks, prylars, and ranjens serve monasteries and shrines across the planet. Faith and politics are not separable on Bajor: kais have contended openly with first ministers, and doctrinal disputes have brought the planet to the edge of civil conflict. The discovery of the wormhole in 2369, and its identification with the Celestial Temple, turned theology into geography. The Prophets acquired an address, their Emissary a uniform, and Bajor found its scripture suddenly entangled with interstellar politics. Records of the noncorporeal beings within the wormhole neither confirm nor deny the whole of the faith; Bajor, on the whole, has not required them to.

sections.heading: The Occupation
sections.body:
In the first half of the twenty-fourth century the Cardassian Union annexed Bajor, beginning an occupation that lasted, by most reckonings, some four decades until the withdrawal of 2369; records differ on when presence became conquest, which is itself a comment on how occupations arrive. The Cardassians came for resources and stayed to strip them. Uridium and other ores were mined and processed, much of the work done aboard the orbital station Terok Nor, using Bajoran forced labor, and camps such as Gallitep became bywords for atrocity. Millions of Bajorans died; millions more were displaced into refugee communities across the quadrant.

Resistance began early and never stopped, fought from the hills and the tunnels by cells whose names are now honored and whose methods are still debated. The occupation collapsed under the weight of that resistance and of Cardassia's own politics, and the withdrawal left Bajor free, wounded, and armed with an unbroken conviction that it had liberated itself. The occupation remains the central fact of modern Bajoran identity, the wound against which every later choice is measured.

sections.heading: Rebuilding and the Provisional Government
sections.body:
The state that emerged from the withdrawal was improvised and said so: a provisional government led by a first minister, with a Chamber of Ministers legislating and the Vedek Assembly exerting a moral authority no statute defines. The Bajoran Militia absorbed much of the resistance and serves as the planet's defense force, its officers carrying the burdens of both histories.

The early years were harsh. The Cardassians had poisoned farmland and gutted infrastructure on their way out, and relief, irrigation, and soil reclamation consumed the government's first budgets alongside the work of repatriating refugees and holding elections that kept being interrupted. The Circle, an isolationist movement, attempted a coup in 2370 with covertly supplied weapons; it failed when the foreign hand behind it was exposed. Federation assistance, requested, resented, and relied upon in shifting proportions, ran through all of it, administered largely from Deep Space 9. That the provisional government remained provisional for years was often mocked; that it held elections, survived coups, and fed its people was the better measure.

sections.heading: The Wormhole and the Emissary
sections.body:
The stable wormhole discovered off Bajor in 2369 rewrote the planet's position in a day. Strategically, it made the Bajoran system the sole gateway to the Gamma Quadrant, courted by every power and coveted by the Dominion. Religiously, it confirmed the Celestial Temple's location and gave the faith a living voice, for the Starfleet officer who first passed through, Benjamin Sisko of Deep Space 9, was recognized by the kai as the Emissary of the Prophets foretold in prophecy.

The Emissary's dual role, Starfleet officer and Bajoran religious figure, was uncomfortable for everyone including him, and records of his tenure trace a slow movement from reluctance to acceptance to something like belief. Bajor's fortunes in the Dominion War turned on both aspects. The Emissary's warning in 2373 led Bajor to sign a nonaggression pact and stand formally aside, sparing the planet a second occupation while the station above it changed hands, and the Prophets' intervention against a Dominion fleet inside the wormhole did the rest. Whatever else is said of the era, Bajor ended the war unconquered.

sections.heading: Toward the Federation
sections.body:
Bajor petitioned for Federation membership in the years after the withdrawal, and the question shaped a decade of its politics. Membership promised security, reconstruction, and standing; opponents saw sovereignty newly won being handed to another distant authority, and the debate ran through elections, the Assembly, and the shrines. The petition was approved in 2373, and then, at the signing ceremony, deferred at the urging of the Emissary, whose warning against joining at that moment was vindicated within months when war broke out and a non-member Bajor could stand behind its pact.

After the war ended in 2375 the path reopened, with the obstacles of wartime removed and Bajor's standing higher than ever. Records from the period indicate the process resumed; accounts differ on when accession was finally completed, but not on its direction, and later references treat Bajor's place within the Federation as settled. The longer meaning is not in dispute. A world that began the century occupied ended it unconquered, courted, and choosing its alliances for itself.

guides.title: Cardassia Prime
guides.summary: Cardassia Prime is the homeworld of the Cardassians and capital of the Cardassian Union — an arid, resource-poor planet whose military state, occupation of Bajor, Dominion alliance and postwar reconstruction reshaped the politics of the Alpha Quadrant.

sections.heading: Planetary Profile and Capital
sections.body:
Cardassia Prime is the principal world of the Cardassian system and the seat of the Cardassian Union. It is a hot planet by the standards of most humanoid species, with an arid climate over much of its landmass and a thin margin of arable ground that has never comfortably fed its population. Cardassians themselves prefer the heat; visitors from temperate worlds find the cities oppressive and the daylight harsh.

The capital, Cardassia City, concentrates the organs of the state: the chambers of the Detapa Council, the headquarters of Central Command, and, for most of the Union's modern history, the unmarked offices of the Obsidian Order. Architecture across the planet follows the same official style — heavy, swept, deliberately monumental — meant to remind the citizen of the state's permanence.

The planet's defining scarcity is material. Cardassia exhausted much of its own mineral wealth generations ago, and the hunger for ore, fuel and food drove the expansion that became the modern Union. Nearly every element of Cardassian policy, from annexation to alliance, traces back in the end to the poverty of the homeworld's soil.

sections.heading: The Union and Its Institutions
sections.body:
The Cardassian Union is formally governed by the Detapa Council, a civilian body, but for most of the last century real authority rested with two rival institutions: Central Command, the military hierarchy, and the Obsidian Order, the intelligence service. Each maintained its own fleets, its own budgets and its own informants, and each watched the other as closely as it watched the Union's enemies.

The Obsidian Order was widely regarded as the most efficient intelligence service in the quadrant, ahead even of the Romulan Tal Shiar. It was said that a citizen could not sit down to a meal without the Order knowing the contents of the plate. Its collapse followed a disastrous joint operation with the Tal Shiar against the Founders in 2371, when a combined fleet was annihilated in the Omarion Nebula.

The Order's fall broke the old balance of power. In 2372 a civilian uprising placed the Detapa Council in genuine control of the state for the first time in living memory — a brief experiment in reform, ended not from within but by the Dominion.

sections.heading: The Occupation of Bajor
sections.body:
The annexation of Bajor stands as the defining act of the modern Union and the crime for which Cardassia is most widely remembered. Cardassian forces formally annexed the planet in the early twenty-fourth century — Bajoran and Cardassian records differ on precisely when the occupation should be dated from — and held it for roughly four decades, strip-mining its resources, conscripting its people into labour camps and working to suppress its religious institutions.

In its final years the occupation was administered from Terok Nor, an ore-processing station in Bajoran orbit under the prefecture of Gul Dukat. Bajoran resistance cells made the planet steadily more expensive to hold, and in 2369 the Union withdrew, officially citing the costs of administration.

Within the Union the occupation was taught as a civilising mission; the famine and the atrocities were absent from official records. The withdrawal was treated as a political humiliation rather than a moral reckoning, a wound that ambitious officers such as Dukat would later exploit. Terok Nor, abandoned in orbit, passed to Bajoran control and Federation administration as the station Deep Space 9.

sections.heading: The Dominion Alliance and the War
sections.body:
In 2373 Gul Dukat, then reduced to commanding a single freighter, secretly negotiated Cardassia's entry into the Dominion. The agreement restored the Union's fleets and Dukat's own power at the price of sovereignty: Dominion forces poured through the Bajoran wormhole, and Cardassia Prime became the Dominion's headquarters in the Alpha Quadrant.

The alliance was sold to the population as restoration. It ended as catastrophe. As the war turned against the Dominion, Cardassian units were spent as expendable assets and dissent at home was answered with reprisals. In the war's final days the Cardassian military turned on its Dominion masters, joining the Federation Alliance in the assault on the homeworld.

The Founders' answer was extermination. Dominion forces levelled Cardassia's cities from orbit and by ground sweep, killing on the order of eight hundred million Cardassians before the surrender was signed in 2375. The capital was rubble; the institutions that had ruled the Union for a century were gone. No world on either side of the war paid a comparable price, and no account of the conflict is complete without saying so.

sections.heading: Society, Family and Culture
sections.body:
Cardassian society before the fall was built on two loyalties, taught from childhood as one: the family and the state. Multi-generational households were the norm, elders were revered, and the education system — among the finest in the quadrant at rote instruction and memory training — produced citizens who could recite the history of the Union exactly as the state preferred it told.

Cardassian arts reflect the same discipline. The most honoured literary form, the repetitive epic, returns to the same events again and again with accumulating variation, prizing endurance and fidelity over surprise. Enigma tales, a popular genre of crime fiction, pose mysteries in which every suspect is guilty and the interest lies in discovering who is guilty of what.

Jurisprudence followed literature. In a Cardassian court the verdict was determined before proceedings opened, and the trial served as public instruction: the accused confessed, the state demonstrated its vigilance, and the audience went home reassured. Archon and conservator alike understood their roles as performers. Offworld observers called it theatre; Cardassians called it order, and a remarkable number of them defended it sincerely.

sections.heading: Reconstruction
sections.body:
The postwar decades have been the hardest in Cardassian history. The Dominion's final bombardment destroyed the planet's infrastructure along with its cities; famine and disease killed uncounted survivors in the first years, and the living dug their dead from the rubble of a capital that had been the proudest architecture in the Union.

Reconstruction proceeded with Federation and allied assistance, accepted unevenly by a population taught for generations to regard dependence as disgrace. Civilian government was rebuilt around a restored Detapa Council, and for the first time in centuries the military served the state rather than constituting it. Veterans of the final uprising against the Dominion occupy an uneasy place in public memory — celebrated as liberators, distrusted as soldiers.

The deeper reconstruction has been cultural. Postwar Cardassian writing broke with the official epic to produce memoir, lament and satire that would have meant imprisonment a generation earlier. Records of the occupation of Bajor, long sealed or falsified, entered public archives, and the first formal exchanges with Bajor followed. Whether the Union that emerges will resemble the old one remains an open question; Cardassians themselves, characteristically, debate it with vigour and at length.

guides.title: Deep Space Nine, the Station
guides.summary: Deep Space 9, the space station at the mouth of the Bajoran wormhole: a Cardassian-built ore-processing station, Terok Nor, turned Federation-administered trade hub, fortress, and the Dominion War's most contested outpost among stations of its era.

sections.heading: From Terok Nor to Deep Space 9
sections.body:
The station was built by the Cardassian Union around 2351, in orbit of Bajor, under the name Terok Nor. Its purpose was the occupation: uridium ore stripped from Bajor was processed in the station's refineries by Bajoran forced labor, while the occupation's administration ran from its upper levels, for years under the prefect Gul Dukat. When the Cardassians withdrew from Bajor in 2369 they gutted the station on their way out, stripping equipment and leaving sabotage behind.

The Bajoran provisional government, holding a claim to the station but lacking the means to run it, invited the Federation to administer it jointly, and Starfleet took up residence under the designation Deep Space 9. Command has been shared ever since: a Starfleet commanding officer, a Bajoran Militia first officer, and a mixed crew in which Federation and Bajoran personnel serve side by side. The arrangement was awkward by design, a station that belongs to Bajor, is run by Starfleet, and was built by the power both parties distrust, and it has functioned anyway.

sections.heading: Structure and Layout
sections.body:
The station follows Cardassian orbital architecture: concentric rings around a central core, with everything curved, ribbed, and deliberately imposing. The core rises through the station's axis, carrying the fusion reactors, the main computer, and, at its crown, the operations center from which the station is run. Around the core's midsection lies the Promenade, the station's public heart. The habitat ring encircles the core, holding quarters for a resident population that runs into the thousands, and the outer docking ring provides ports for freighters and runabouts, with six great docking pylons sweeping up and down from its rim to take larger starships.

Cardassian design choices persist everywhere. Door mechanisms, computer interfaces, and security systems all speak their builders' language, and Starfleet engineers spent years persuading Cardassian hardware to run Federation software. The station was built as a factory and a fortress, not a home, and every improvement since has been an argument with its architecture, an argument its residents, on the whole, have won.

sections.heading: The Wormhole Changes Everything
sections.body:
Weeks after Starfleet took command in 2369, the station's purpose changed permanently. In the nearby Denorios Belt, station officers discovered the only known stable wormhole: a fixed passage some seventy thousand light-years long, connecting the Bajoran system to the distant Gamma Quadrant. To Bajoran faith the discovery was not an anomaly but a confirmation, the Celestial Temple of the Prophets, exactly where scripture had placed it.

The station was moved at once from Bajor orbit to the mouth of the wormhole to secure the claim, and what had been a battered relic of the occupation became one of the most strategically significant positions in the quadrant. Commerce arrived first: freighters, prospectors, scientists, and pilgrims, making the station a crossroads and Bajor a destination. Contact with Gamma Quadrant civilizations followed. So, in time, did the Dominion. Every later chapter of the station's history, its prosperity, its fortification, its capture and recapture, follows from the single fact of what sits at its doorstep.

sections.heading: Life on the Promenade
sections.body:
The Promenade wraps the station's core in two levels of shops, offices, and public rooms, and its daily crowd is the station's character in miniature. A Bajoran shrine stands within sight of the infirmary and the security office; the schoolroom, the replimat, and the assay office share foot traffic with traders from three quadrants. The best-known establishment is Quark's, bar, gaming house, and holosuite operation, whose Ferengi proprietor has been part of station life since the occupation years. Residents have included Bajoran clergy and militia, Starfleet families, Cardassian holdouts, and a tailor whose past is a matter of record and dispute.

The station's social texture is unlike a starship's. It has permanent civilians, commerce, crime, worship, and politics, and its Starfleet officers govern as much as they command. Records of the station's civic life, its festivals, elections, labor disputes, and one long-running darts rivalry, sit alongside its military logs, and any honest account of Deep Space 9 gives the Promenade equal weight with the pylons.

sections.heading: Fortress at the Threshold
sections.body:
The station's armament was an afterthought until the threats arrived. Facing Dominion pressure and then a Klingon assault in 2372, Starfleet rebuilt Deep Space 9 as a fortress, fitting rotating batteries of phasers and torpedo launchers into the rings and pylons and stockpiling thousands of torpedoes; the upgrades were proven when the station held off a Klingon fleet at its docking clamps.

In late 2373 the Dominion took the station at the war's opening, the Federation withdrawing only after sealing the wormhole's mouth behind a field of self-replicating mines, and it served the enemy under its old name, Terok Nor, until Operation Return retook it months later, with the Prophets themselves intervening to erase a Dominion fleet inside the wormhole. For the rest of the war the station was the Federation's forward anchor, staging the Chin'toka offensives and repairing the ships that came back. The war ended where much of it had begun: the instrument of surrender, the Treaty of Bajor, was signed aboard the station in 2375.

guides.title: Ferenginar
guides.summary: Ferenginar is the rain-soaked homeworld of the Ferengi and seat of the Ferengi Alliance — the planet of the Grand Nagus and the Tower of Commerce, the Rules of Acquisition, commerce as culture, and the reforms that remade Ferengi society.

sections.heading: A World of Rain
sections.body:
Ferenginar, homeworld of the Ferengi and capital of the Ferengi Alliance, is a temperate planet distinguished above all by rain. Precipitation falls over most of the planet on most days of the year; the Ferengi language is said to contain well over a hundred words for rain and none at all for crisp, and the customary greeting on arrival wishes the visitor profitable shelter. Swamps, deltas and flooded lowlands dominate the geography, and Ferengi architecture answers with domes, covered arcades and drainage engineering of genuine magnificence.

The capital centres on the Tower of Commerce, the tallest structure on the planet and the seat of the Grand Nagus, rising over the Sacred Marketplace. Pilgrims — the word is used without irony — travel from across the Alliance to see it, paying admission at every stage of the visit, including a modest fee to sit in the waiting room, which is itself described as an honour.

Offworlders often find the climate miserable and the fees astonishing. Ferengi find both remarks equally baffling. The rain, they point out, is free; it would be an act of civic negligence to let anything else be.

sections.heading: The Grand Nagus and the Alliance
sections.body:
The Ferengi Alliance is governed — managed, a Ferengi would say — by the Grand Nagus, an office combining head of state, chief executive and market oracle in a single set of lobes. The Nagus sets economic policy, licenses trade routes by sale, arbitrates the largest commercial disputes, and is traditionally attended by a silent Hupyrian servant. His staff of office, topped with a gold likeness of his own head, is kissed by petitioners as a mark of respect.

Beneath the Nagus sit the Congress of Economic Advisors and a bureaucracy whose most feared arm is the Ferengi Commerce Authority. FCA liquidators audit, license and, where necessary, ruin: a citizen whose practices are judged insufficiently Ferengi may see his assets seized and his contracts voided, a civic death many consider worse than the ordinary kind.

Succession is by designation rather than inheritance, and the retirement of a Nagus reliably triggers a frenzy of positioning. The most consequential modern holder of the office was Grand Nagus Zek, whose long rule ended in 2375 with reforms that scandalised half the Alliance — and with his choice of the famously mild engineer Rom as successor, which scandalised the other half.

sections.heading: The Rules of Acquisition
sections.body:
The Rules of Acquisition are the closest thing Ferengi civilisation has to scripture: a numbered collection of commercial precepts — 285 in the modern canon — governing everything from contract discipline to family relations and interstellar diplomacy. War, one Rule observes, is good for business; another immediately notes that peace is good for business; and the tension between them is considered a complete education in statecraft.

Tradition holds that the first Rule was set down by Gint, the first Grand Nagus, and that the collection's very title was a marketing decision — rules sold better than suggestions would have. Every Ferengi child memorises them; every Ferengi adult cites them the way other cultures cite law, proverb and poetry at once, and disagreement over which Rule governs a situation is the foundation of Ferengi jurisprudence and of after-dinner argument alike.

Scholars note that the Rules contradict one another freely, and that this is regarded as a feature: the wise Ferengi knows which Rule the moment requires. Unofficial commentaries, apocryphal rules and outright forgeries circulate constantly, and the authenticated editions — sold, naturally, at a healthy margin — remain among the most reliably profitable publications in the quadrant.

sections.heading: Commerce as Culture
sections.body:
On Ferenginar, commerce is not one sector of life; it is the medium of all of it. Status is measured in profit, contracts stand where other cultures place vows, and small ritual payments accompany every social occasion: guests entering a Ferengi home pay a token admission, and the traditional greeting formula politely acknowledges the host's ownership of everything in sight.

Ferengi religion is commercial to its core. The dead are believed to face the Blessed Exchequer, who audits the ledger of a lifetime; the profitable ascend to the Divine Treasury, while the insolvent are consigned to the Vault of Eternal Destitution. In preparation, Ferengi of standing sell futures on their own remains, which are vacuum-desiccated after death and marketed in collectible portions to admirers and creditors alike.

Underlying all of this is a genuinely sophisticated economic philosophy. The Great Material Continuum — the great river, as it is taught — holds that every world in the galaxy has too much of something and too little of something else, and that the skilled trader navigates the flow between them. Ferengi commerce, at its best, is that navigation, and even the culture's sternest critics concede that the river delivers.

sections.heading: Reform and the New Ferenginar
sections.body:
For most of its history the Alliance denied economic personhood to half its population. Ferengi females were barred from earning profit, holding property, travelling freely or wearing clothes; the traditional ideal confined them to the home, chewing food for their sons. The system was defended as both sacred and efficient, and was neither.

Its unravelling was rapid by Ferengi standards. In the early 2370s Ishka — mother of the barkeeper and entrepreneur Quark and of the engineer Rom — earned profit in open defiance of the law and, rather than submit to confiscation, took her case to Grand Nagus Zek himself. She won considerably more than the case. As Zek's adviser and companion she pushed through amendments permitting females to wear clothing and to earn profit, over furious conservative resistance that briefly cost Zek his office.

Zek's later reforms went further: progressive taxation, labour protections and curbs on monopoly, capped by his retirement and the elevation of Rom in 2375. Traditionalists prophesied ruin; the ruin declined to arrive. The Alliance that entered the postwar era remained gleefully acquisitive, but a Ferengi daughter born after the reforms inherited what her grandmother had been forbidden even to touch: a ledger of her own.

guides.title: Risa
guides.summary: Risa is the Federation's celebrated pleasure planet — a resort world of engineered perfect weather, Risian hospitality, the horga'hn and jamaharon customs, and a tourist economy that draws travellers from across the quadrant.

sections.heading: The Paradise That Was Built
sections.body:
Risa's perfection is a public work. The planet's natural condition is by all accounts dismal — tectonically restless and soaked by near-continuous tropical rain — and its transformation into the quadrant's byword for paradise is an engineering achievement of the first order. A planet-wide network of weather control stations and seismic regulators maintains the climate advertised in every brochure: warm days, gentle nights, and rain permitted only where and when a landscape needs it.

The system's scale is easy to underestimate from a beach chair. Weather modification grids manage atmospheric circulation across entire hemispheres; seismic dampers quiet a crust that would otherwise shake the resorts into the sea. Risians speak of the network with the mixture of pride and dependence that other worlds reserve for their fleets.

The dependence is real. On the rare occasions the network has been disabled — most notoriously by political sabotage in 2373 — the planet reverts within hours to storms and tremors, an unsubtle reminder that paradise on Risa is not a place but an ongoing decision, renewed continuously by people who are very good at their jobs.

sections.heading: The Risian People and Their Hospitality
sections.body:
The Risians are a humanoid people recognisable by the small gold emblem worn on the forehead, and famous for a culture in which hospitality is not an industry but an ethic. The phrase that greets every arrival — all that is ours is yours — is meant substantially: guests are treated with a warmth and attentiveness that first-time visitors from more reserved cultures often mistake for something else, and occasionally, to their considerable embarrassment, are not mistaken.

Risian society is open about intimacy and unembarrassed by pleasure, an attitude grounded in a philosophy that treats rest, sensuality and play as necessities of a healthy life rather than indulgences to be rationed. Visitors are never obliged to participate in anything; the famous openness runs entirely on invitation and consent, and Risian hosts are expert at reading which invitations to extend, and to whom.

Beneath the warmth is professionalism. The hospitality corps trains for years, the guest-services guilds hold standards that would flatter a Starfleet inspection, and the planet's gentle manner has never prevented its authorities from removing, swiftly and permanently, the rare visitor who mistakes generosity for weakness.

sections.heading: The Horga'hn and the Jamaharon
sections.body:
The horga'hn is Risa's most recognisable object: a small carved totem, the traditional symbol of fertility, sold, gifted and collected across the Federation. On Risa itself it retains a precise social function. To display a horga'hn openly is to declare oneself seeking jamaharon, and travellers are warned — by guidebooks, by friends, and eventually by experience — to be quite sure the declaration is intended before setting one on a bar.

What jamaharon itself is, outsiders are cheerfully left to wonder. Risians describe it only as a celebration of shared pleasure whose particulars are a matter between hosts and guest; offworld speculation ranges from the plausible to the anatomically ambitious, and Risians decline to referee. The discretion is itself the custom: what happens within jamaharon is not discussed outside it.

The etiquette surrounding these customs is simple and strictly observed. Nothing is assumed, nothing is owed, and a declined invitation costs nothing but the moment. Visitors who buy a horga'hn as a souvenir are advised to carry it wrapped — a rule famously learned the hard way by more than one Starfleet officer whose well-meaning friends knew exactly what they were doing.

sections.heading: Tourism: What Risa Offers
sections.body:
Risa offers rest at every level of ambition. The famous resorts line coasts engineered for them — Suraya Bay and the Temtibi Lagoon appear in half the travel literature of the Federation — with steam pools, subterranean gardens and beaches whose sand temperature is a managed variable. Guests who want exertion can find it: hoverball, sailing, diving, and the cliff face called Galartha, which alters its pitch while being climbed and is therefore never the same ascent twice.

Festivals punctuate the calendar, most famously the Lohlunat, the Festival of the Moons, which fills the coasts each year. Cuisine is cosmopolitan by policy: Risian kitchens hold that a guest's comfort includes the tastes of home, and the great resorts can produce a credible version of almost any world's table on a day's notice.

The clientele is as mixed as the quadrant. Starfleet crews on shore leave, Ferengi entrepreneurs conducting meetings of unusual length, diplomats recovering from one another — Risa hosts them all under the same standing rule: disputes, ranks and wars are checked at the port of entry. The planet's neutrality is informal but jealously kept, and by long habit even hereditary enemies manage, on Risa, to share a beach.

sections.heading: Incidents and Interruptions
sections.body:
Paradise keeps an incident log like everywhere else. In 2152 the Earth starship Enterprise NX-01 called at Risa during its first deep-space cruise, and members of its crew, exploring the port district's less curated quarters, were robbed by criminals posing as friendly locals — an early lesson that even a welcoming world has alleys.

In 2366 Risa hosted a stranger affair: agents from the twenty-seventh century arrived seeking the Tox Uthat, a stolen future weapon hidden on the planet, drawing a vacationing Captain Jean-Luc Picard into its recovery and eventual destruction. Risian authorities note, correctly, that none of the parties involved were Risian.

The most pointed interruption came in 2373, when the New Essentialists, a Federation political movement, sabotaged the weather grid to demonstrate that the Federation had gone soft behind its comforts.
