Storms returned within hours; sympathy for the argument did not. The grid was restored, the movement subsided into obscurity, and Risa drew from the episode the only conclusion it has ever drawn from adversity: the guests must be looked after, and the rain must be put back where it belongs.

guides.title: The Badlands
guides.summary: The Badlands are a region of violent plasma storms near the Cardassian border — a hazard to starships and navigation, a haven for the Maquis, smugglers and spies, and the place where the USS Voyager vanished.

sections.heading: A Region of Storms
sections.body:
The Badlands are a compact region of space lying close to the border between Cardassian and Federation territory, notorious across two quadrants for weather no planet could match. The region is filled with continuous plasma storms: rivers and funnels of charged plasma that twist through the volume in patterns no model has ever fully predicted, punctuated by intense gravitational anomalies that bend safe headings into lethal ones without warning.

The origin of the storms remains unsettled. Survey data are, for obvious reasons, incomplete; the leading accounts invoke interactions between dense interstellar plasma fields and the region's anomalous gravitation, but the Badlands have defeated every systematic attempt at mapping. Charts of the interior are sold, traded and forged all along the border, and every experienced pilot regards all of them as fiction with footnotes.

What is settled is the region's reputation. Sensor range inside the Badlands collapses to a fraction of normal, communications are unreliable, and a vessel in trouble is effectively beyond assistance. Prudent traffic gives the region a wide berth — which is precisely why so much of the border's history has been made by those who did not.

sections.heading: Flying the Badlands
sections.body:
Standard fleet doctrine on the Badlands runs to one word: avoid. Vessels that enter anyway do so slowly and humbly. High warp is suicidal in the interior; plasma density and gravitational shear make sustained warp fields unstable, so transits are flown at impulse or the lowest warp factors, hugging the calmer channels between storm cells. Shields are run continuously against discharge strikes, which can disable an unwary ship in a single contact.

Detection works both ways. The same interference that blinds a pursuer conceals the pursued, and a small, agile vessel with a bold pilot can use a plasma funnel the way groundside fugitives use weather — as a door that closes behind them. Large warships, with their deep warp fields and wide sensor cross-sections, are at a systematic disadvantage, a fact with heavy consequences in the region's political history.

Losses are constant and often unexplained. Ships vanish in the Badlands without wreckage, and border folklore populates the interior generously with ghosts. Investigators note dryly that plasma storms rarely leave debris to find — and that not every disappearance in the Badlands necessarily happened because of the Badlands.

sections.heading: Refuge of the Maquis
sections.body:
The Badlands entered political history in the 2370s as the sanctuary of the Maquis, the movement of Federation-born colonists who took up arms against Cardassia after the border treaty of 2370 placed their worlds inside the Cardassian Demilitarized Zone. Maquis cells based ships, supplies and training camps inside the storms, where Cardassian patrols could not follow in strength and Starfleet could not easily police its own citizens.

The geography suited the insurgency perfectly. Lightly armed raiders and converted couriers, flown by pilots willing to skim plasma funnels, could strike into the Zone and disappear; both Central Command and Starfleet lost pursuing vessels to storms that swallowed the chase. For roughly three years the Badlands functioned as the Maquis capital in everything but name, and the movement's leaders planned from places no chart admitted existed.

The sanctuary failed against a different enemy. When the Dominion took control of Cardassia in 2373, its forces swept the Badlands with numbers and thoroughness no Alpha Quadrant power had ever spent there, and the Maquis were effectively annihilated within weeks. Survivors scattered or were imprisoned; the storms keep what remains of their bases.

sections.heading: The Voyager Disappearance
sections.body:
The most famous vessel ever lost in the Badlands was not, in the end, lost to them. In 2371 the USS Voyager, an Intrepid-class starship under Captain Kathryn Janeway, entered the region in pursuit of a Maquis raider commanded by the former Starfleet officer Chakotay. Both ships vanished. Starfleet's search found no wreckage, and in time both crews were declared missing and then dead.

The truth emerged years later: both vessels had been seized from inside the Badlands by a coherent tetryon beam and displaced some seventy thousand light-years into the Delta Quadrant by an entity known as the Caretaker. The two crews, insurgent and pursuer, completed the journey home as a single company over seven years — a story told in full elsewhere in this database.

The incident permanently altered the region's reputation. What had been a navigational hazard acquired a stranger record: proof that the storms could hide not only smugglers and rebels but phenomena capable of reaching across the galaxy. Subsequent surveys found no trace of the displacement mechanism, and the Badlands have yielded no comparable event since. Traffic advisories note this with limited reassurance.

sections.heading: Smugglers, Spies and Strategy
sections.body:
Beyond rebellion and shipwreck, the Badlands serve every trade that profits from being unobserved. Smuggling routes thread the storm margins, where a cargo can be cached inside an outer cell and retrieved by whoever holds the coordinates; contraband runners working the Cardassian and Bajoran approaches used the region long before the Federation charted it, and criminal brokerages have bought and sold safe channels like commodities.

Intelligence services follow the smugglers. The storms' sensor shadow makes them a natural venue for covert rendezvous, dead drops and deniable meetings, and more than one border incident officially attributed to plasma discharge is privately attributed, in several capitals at once, to something with a hull.

In open war the region's value inverted. During the Dominion War the Badlands anchored a flank neither side could hold or fully scout: minefields and listening posts ringed the approaches, and fleet movements on both sides were planned around the storms as around a fortress that no army owned. Postwar traffic has settled back into the old pattern — freighters keeping their distance, patrols keeping their logs vague, and the storms keeping, as they always have, whatever enters them unprepared.

guides.title: The Utopia Planitia Fleet Yards
guides.summary: The Utopia Planitia Fleet Yards were Starfleet's principal shipyards, in orbit of Mars and on its surface — birthplace of the Galaxy, Defiant and Intrepid classes and the USS Voyager, and the target of the synth attack of 2385.

sections.heading: Starfleet's Shipyard
sections.body:
The Utopia Planitia Fleet Yards were for most of the twenty-fourth century Starfleet's premier shipbuilding complex, and among the largest industrial undertakings in Federation history. The facility was double-sited: a constellation of orbital drydocks, spaceframe gantries and fabrication stations in synchronous orbit above Mars, paired with surface works on the Utopia Planitia plain below, where major components were forged, tested and lifted to orbit.

Mars had been central to human spaceflight since the earliest colonial era, and the yards grew with the Federation itself. At their height they employed Starfleet engineers, civilian specialists and, in the final years, synthetic labourers numbering in the thousands, with entire habitat rings and surface settlements existing solely to support the work.

To serve at Utopia Planitia was a distinction in Starfleet's engineering branch. The yards were not merely an assembly site but a proving ground where doctrine met metal: new hull geometries, computer cores and propulsion systems were trialled there before any of them bore a registry number. Generations of chief engineers describe the same first impression from the shuttle window — drydock frames like cathedral ribs, catching the thin Martian sunrise.

sections.heading: The Ships
sections.body:
The catalogue of Utopia Planitia reads like a history of the modern fleet. The yards headquartered the Galaxy-class development project, the most ambitious spaceframe programme of its era, and the class's early hulls — among them the USS Enterprise NCC-1701-D — took shape in its drydocks. The same complex developed the Defiant class, Starfleet's first purpose-built warship, conceived against the Borg and proven at Deep Space 9; and it built the Intrepid class, including the USS Voyager, launched in 2371 and lost and recovered in the most famous long-range cruise ever logged.

Beyond the celebrated names, the yards' daily bread was the working fleet: tenders, surveyors, runabouts, refits, and the unglamorous mid-life overhauls that keep a navy real. Yard crews took particular pride in refit work, holding that building a new ship is easier than convincing an old one.

By the 2380s the yards carried the heaviest burden in their history: emergency construction of the armada intended to evacuate the Romulan populations threatened by the impending supernova of their sun. Ten thousand engineers and thousands of synthetic workers drove the largest single shipbuilding effort the Federation had ever attempted.

sections.heading: Life and Work at the Yards
sections.body:
A shipyard is a culture as much as a facility, and Utopia Planitia's was distinct: methodical, proud and unsentimental about everything except ships. Design teams and construction crews worked in deliberate friction — the bureaus drawing what ought to be possible, the yard proving what actually was — and the yards' review boards were famously merciless about the difference. Propulsion specialists such as Dr. Leah Brahms of the Galaxy-class programme became quiet legends whose design notes were studied aboard the very ships they shaped, sometimes by engineers in the middle of emergencies.

The workforce lived with Mars rather than merely above it. Orbital crews rotated through surface habitats; yard families raised children in the domed settlements; and First Contact Day, commemorating humanity's first meeting with the Vulcans, was kept as a yard-wide holiday — a detail that would later acquire terrible significance.

In the yards' final years much of the heavy and hazardous labour was performed by synthetics: android workers of limited cognition, built for the task and certified as non-sentient tools. Veterans of the period recall them the way earlier generations recalled industrial replicators — right up until the day that comparison stopped being possible.

sections.heading: First Contact Day, 2385
sections.body:
On First Contact Day in 2385 — a holiday, with much of the workforce standing down — the synthetic labourers turned. In near-unison the yards' synths abandoned their tasks, brought down Mars's orbital defence grid from within, and struck the complex they had helped to build. The drydocks were destroyed with the rescue armada inside them; the surface works were shattered; and the assault ignited flammable vapours in the Martian stratosphere, setting fires that burned for years afterward and were visible from Earth. More than ninety-two thousand people were killed. The armada for the Romulan evacuation was gone within the hour.

The attacking synths destroyed themselves as the assault concluded, erasing the clearest evidence of what had moved them. The official inquiry found catastrophic corruption in their operating code, and the Federation's answer was absolute: a ban on the creation and possession of synthetic life, enforced across every member world.

The verdict did not hold. Investigation years later established that the synths had been subverted by the Zhat Vash, a Romulan faction sworn to destroy artificial life, with the deliberate aim of provoking exactly the ban that followed. The attack achieved precisely what its hidden authors intended — a fact the Federation would not learn for fourteen years.

sections.heading: Aftermath and Legacy
sections.body:
The attack's consequences reshaped the Federation. The rescue armada could not be rebuilt in time, and Starfleet — over the furious objection of the mission's commander, Admiral Jean-Luc Picard — abandoned the Romulan evacuation, a decision that drove Picard's resignation and stained Federation credibility for a generation. Synthetic research was outlawed outright, ending careers and closing institutes across the member worlds.

Mars itself remained scarred, its upper atmosphere still burning years after the attack, a wound in the sky visible from Earth's orbit. The yards were not rebuilt in their old form; shipbuilding dispersed to other facilities, and Utopia Planitia passed from working shipyard to memorial, its wrecked gantries left in orbit for years as both hazard and monument.

Vindication of a kind came in 2399, when the events surrounding the synthetic colony at Coppelius exposed the Zhat Vash conspiracy and demonstrated that synthetic life posed no inherent threat. The ban was repealed. The dead of Mars, organic and synthetic alike, are remembered together on First Contact Day — the holiday the attack was timed to desecrate, kept now with a double meaning the yards' builders never intended.

guides.title: Earth and the Sol System
guides.summary: Earth, Sol and the Federation capital: the seat of the Council and Starfleet Command, and the awkwardness of a union of equals headquartered on one member's homeworld.

sections.heading: Earth in the Federation
sections.body: Earth is one founding member among several, and it is also where the Federation Council sits, where Starfleet Command is headquartered, and where Starfleet Academy trains its officers. That concentration is a standing source of quiet friction: a union of equals whose administrative centre, military headquarters and officer school are all on one member's homeworld invites the charge that it is a human project wearing a wider name, and the charge is made inside the setting more than once. The defence offered is historical accident and convenience rather than principle. Earth was centrally placed among the founding powers, had recently emerged from a period that left it unusually committed to the idea of union, and offered to host. None of which fully answers the objection. Earth itself is described as having been substantially repaired. Its cities are rebuilt, its climate managed, its poverty and its wars ended — a state the setting presents as the outcome of a deliberate century of work following a catastrophe, not as a natural progression.

sections.heading: San Francisco and the Institutions
sections.body: The Presidio at San Francisco holds Starfleet Command and the Academy, with the Council seated nearby. The choice of a single terrestrial city for all of it is one of the setting's more consequential pieces of geography, because it means a strike on one place can decapitate the Federation's civil and military leadership simultaneously — a vulnerability the stories exploit more than once. Utopia Planitia, in orbit of Mars, is the Federation's principal shipyard, and the pairing is deliberate: the institution that decides is on one world and the industry that builds is on another, several light-minutes away. The system also holds the Federation's oldest and densest civilian infrastructure — the transport network, the archives, the research institutes — which is why so many episodes that need a hearing, a trial, a court martial or an admiral bring the ship home.

sections.heading: Getting Here From Elsewhere
sections.body: Sol is a long way from most of the Federation's frontier, which matters constantly. A ship recalled to Earth is a ship removed from its station for weeks, and an order issued from Earth reaches the frontier already out of date. That lag is the practical reason starship captains hold the discretion they do, and the practical reason the frontier periodically complains that the core legislates for conditions it does not experience. The system is heavily defended and heavily monitored, and the setting treats any breach of it as an emergency of the first order. Sequences in which something hostile reaches Earth orbit are used sparingly and always signal that the situation has exceeded what a starship can resolve.

sections.heading: What Earth Represents
sections.body: Within the fiction Earth functions as the argument's exhibit. A civilisation that was, within living historical memory, poor, violent and close to ruining itself is now the administrative centre of an interstellar union — which is offered as evidence that the Federation's optimism is a description of something achieved rather than a hope. The setting is careful not to make that comfortable. The recovery is repeatedly shown to have been hard, contested and recent, and the institutions built on it are shown to be capable of backsliding under pressure. Earth is not written as having transcended its history; it is written as having decided about it, and as having to keep deciding.

guides.title: Starbases and Deep-Space Stations
guides.summary: The fixed points: what a starbase is for, and why a station at a crossroads produces different stories than a ship.

sections.heading: What a Starbase Does
sections.body: A starbase is the Federation's fixed presence in a region: a repair yard, a supply depot, a hospital, a court, a headquarters and a diplomatic post, usually all at once. Some are orbital structures, some are built on planetary surfaces, and their numbering is a long-running administrative sequence rather than a geographic one. For a starship the starbase is the place where the things a ship cannot do for itself get done: a damaged hull replaced, a crew rotated, a court martial heard, a prisoner transferred, an admiral consulted in person. The recurring narrative use is as punctuation — a ship arriving at a starbase marks the end of a situation, and a ship being ordered to one usually means somebody is in trouble. They are also where the Federation's bureaucracy becomes visible. A starship is a community with a captain; a starbase has departments, records offices, requisition procedures and an administrative culture, and the friction between the two is a reliable source of comedy and of genuine obstruction.

sections.heading: A Station at a Crossroads
sections.body: The setting's most fully developed station is one positioned beside a stable passage to an otherwise unreachable region — a fixed point at a genuine strategic crossroads, jointly significant to several powers, and administered by the Federation on behalf of a world that has only recently emerged from occupation. A station cannot leave, and that single constraint changes every story told there. A starship that meets a problem can solve it and move on; a station has to live beside the consequences. Its residents include people who are not Federation citizens, do not share Federation values and have no intention of adopting them, and the administrator's job is therefore politics rather than command. It also inverts the format's usual direction. Instead of a crew travelling out to encounter the galaxy, the galaxy arrives — traders, refugees, spies, pilgrims and fleets — and the drama comes from who has just docked.

sections.heading: Life Aboard
sections.body: A large station is a town. It has a promenade of shops and bars, a temple, a school, an infirmary, a security office and a permanent civilian population with no rank and no orders. Children grow up there. Businesses fail there. Somebody has to decide who gets which docking bay. That civilian texture is what distinguishes station stories from ship stories most sharply. Aboard a starship almost everyone is a Starfleet officer under the same discipline; aboard a station most people are not, and the Federation's authority over them is negotiated rather than assumed. The recurring figure of the resident trader who is technically subject to nobody exists to keep testing exactly that boundary.

sections.heading: Why the Fixed Points Matter
sections.body: Strategically the stations are what make the Federation a polity rather than a fleet. A civilisation whose only presence in a region is a ship passing through does not actually hold that region; a base with repair capacity, a hospital and a garrison does. Narratively they supply the thing a starship format structurally lacks: consequence. A ship that solves a planet's crisis and warps away never learns what happened next. A station watches the next twenty years of it, and the setting uses that to ask harder questions than the travelling format can — about occupation, about collaboration, about what a principle costs when you cannot leave the people it applies to.

guides.title: The Neutral Zones
guides.summary: Bands of space nobody may enter — the Romulan and Klingon Neutral Zones: what they are for, and why the setting keeps returning to them.

sections.heading: A Border Made of Emptiness
sections.body: A neutral zone is a band of space along a contested frontier that both parties agree to keep empty. Entry by a vessel of either power constitutes an act of war by treaty, without further argument required. The Federation maintains such zones with more than one neighbour, the Romulan one being the most consequential and the Klingon one the most frequently violated before that relationship changed. The device is elegant precisely because it is crude. Two powers unable to agree on anything else can agree on a line, and the emptiness on either side of it means that a violation is unambiguous. There is no need to establish intent when the mere presence of a warship is the offence. Zones are monitored rather than garrisoned. Outposts sit along the boundary watching, and their destruction — a well-established opening move in the setting — is how a long silence becomes a crisis in a single scene.

sections.heading: Why It Is Unstable by Design
sections.body: A neutral zone freezes a conflict rather than resolving it. It records that two powers stopped fighting, says nothing about why they were fighting, and leaves every underlying grievance in place with a line drawn over the top. That makes it durable for decades and brittle at the wrong moment. The instability is structural. Both sides must patrol their own edge, which means armed vessels operating within minutes of a tripwire. Both sides run intelligence operations across it, since the emptiness that makes violations obvious also makes surveillance essential. And both sides know that whoever crosses first has the advantage of surprise, which is a permanent incentive nobody can disarm. It also creates a peculiar sort of ignorance. A power that has not seen its neighbour for generations does not know what that neighbour has become — what they now fly, what they now want, or whether the government that signed the treaty still exists. Long neutral zones produce first contact between old enemies, which the setting exploits repeatedly.

sections.heading: Life Along the Line
sections.body: The zones are not quite empty of people. Colonies sit near the boundary, sometimes older than the treaty that drew it, occasionally on the wrong side of a line agreed by governments a long way off. Their inhabitants have views about that, and the setting's border stories are frequently about civilians who did not vote for the arrangement they live under. Postings along a neutral zone are the fleet's least glamorous and most nerve-racking. The work is watching an empty screen for years, and the professional hazard is the opposite of boredom's usual one: an officer who has watched nothing happen for a decade may be slow to believe it when something finally does. Trade, smuggling and unsanctioned contact happen anyway, because a line that neither side can physically seal will be crossed by anyone with a small ship and a reason. Much of the setting's frontier colour comes from that traffic.

sections.heading: When the Line Moves
sections.body: Neutral zones end in one of three ways. They are overrun, which is war. They are dissolved by agreement, which requires the underlying quarrel to have been settled or overtaken by something larger — the usual something larger being a threat that makes both parties prefer each other to the alternative. Or they simply persist, unresolved, until the powers on either side have changed enough that the original terms mean nothing. The Klingon zone is the setting's example of the second case, dissolved after decades of hostility when circumstances made the alliance obviously preferable. The Romulan one is the example of the third: honoured with rigid formality across a silence long enough for both sides to become strangers, then broken and re-established more than once. What the device gives the setting is a frontier with a permanent question mark on it. Every story set near one starts with the audience already knowing that crossing is unthinkable, which means any reason good enough to consider it is by definition a serious one.

guides.title: Vulcan, the Planet
guides.summary: The world itself: heat, thin air, high gravity, and a landscape that shaped a philosophy.

sections.heading: Conditions
sections.body: Vulcan is hot, arid and heavy. Its surface temperatures are punishing to most humanoids, its atmosphere is thinner than Earth's, and its gravity is appreciably higher — a combination that leaves visitors breathless, dehydrated and tired within hours, and which requires acclimatisation or assistance for anything more than a short stay. The landscape is largely desert: red rock, vast dune fields, mountain ranges and deep canyon systems, with what water there is concentrated and precious. Vegetation is sparse and adapted, and the animal life includes several genuinely dangerous predators. Nothing about the world is gentle. Its sky is notable enough to be a recurring detail. Vulcan's sun is bright and its nights are not dark in the way Earth's are, which the setting uses whenever it wants to make an offworld visitor feel unmistakably elsewhere.

sections.heading: The Landscape as Argument
sections.body: Vulcan philosophy is usually explained through its history, and the setting is careful to show that the geography did as much work. A civilisation on a world this hostile, with limited water and violent weather, must cooperate precisely or die, and its ethical tradition treats discipline as survival rather than as virtue for its own sake. The desert also supplies the culture's central metaphor. Its most demanding rite of passage sends an adolescent alone into the wilderness for days with minimal equipment, and the landscape is genuinely capable of killing them. A society that requires this of its children is making a claim about what it thinks people are for. Vulcan monasteries and retreats sit in the least habitable places deliberately. The tradition holds that a mind is trained where the body is uncomfortable, which is an idea with terrestrial parallels and which the setting presents without irony.

sections.heading: Cities and Institutions
sections.body: Vulcan settlement is concentrated, ancient and built for the climate: thick walls, deep shade, water managed with the seriousness of a civilisation that has been short of it for millennia. Its architecture is described as austere and monumental, and its cities are old enough that particular buildings have been continuously in use for thousands of years. The world hosts institutions of considerable weight — the Vulcan Science Academy foremost among them, whose standards are formidable and whose rejection of a candidate is a serious matter. A great deal of the Federation's scientific output originates here, and Vulcan expertise is one of the things the coalition was founded to share. There is also a diplomatic establishment of long standing. Vulcan conducted interstellar relations for a century before most of its neighbours, and its embassies, protocols and institutional memory shaped how the Federation does the same.

sections.heading: Visiting
sections.body: Offworlders on Vulcan are common and never quite comfortable. Federation facilities maintain adjusted environments, and visitors are advised to acclimatise, to respect the water conventions, and to observe the local prohibition on casual physical contact — a matter of real consequence with a touch-telepathic people rather than a point of etiquette. Vulcan hospitality is formal, precise and easily misread as cold. Guests are provided for exactly and not fussed over, questions are answered directly, and the absence of small talk is not disapproval. Visitors who expect warmth read the reception as a rebuff; those who expect precision find it generous. The setting sends its characters there at moments of gravity — a family matter, a rite, a crisis of identity — and the world's difficulty is part of why. Vulcan is somewhere you go to do something serious, and it does not make it easy.

guides.title: Qo'noS, the Klingon Homeworld
guides.summary: Qo'noS, also written Qonos and spoken as Kronos: a harsh world and the seat of an empire — geography, the Great Houses, and the politics of the High Council.

sections.heading: The World
sections.body: Qo'noS is a world of extremes — violent weather, heavy seismic activity, an axial tilt that produces punishing seasons, and terrain that runs to mountain, volcanic waste and dense forest rather than to anything comfortable. Its skies are frequently overcast and its atmosphere heavier than most humanoids prefer. Klingon culture treats this as a point of pride rather than a hardship. A world that kills the careless is understood to have produced a people worth respecting, and the setting's Klingons describe visitors' discomfort with undisguised satisfaction. The planet lost a moon within recorded history — the disaster that crippled the Empire's energy production and forced the peace with the Federation. The astronomical consequence alone reshaped the world's tides and weather, and the political consequence reshaped the quadrant. It is the rare case where a planetary event and a diplomatic one are the same event.

sections.heading: The Great Houses
sections.body: Klingon society organises around houses: extended kin groups holding land, fleets, seats and obligations, headed by a leader whose standing is the house's standing. Individual honour and family honour are not separable, which means one member's disgrace is inherited by relatives who had nothing to do with it, and one member's achievement raises everyone. This produces politics that look feudal and are in fact intensely legalistic. Challenges, claims, inheritances, discommendations and restorations all follow procedure, and a Klingon with a grievance is as likely to pursue it through a council of elders as through a duel. Both are available and both are honourable. House politics also supply the Empire's chronic instability. Houses rise and fall by manoeuvre as much as by combat, alliances are transactional, and a High Council seat is worth a great deal to a family that has one. The setting's Klingon stories are far more often about this than about war.

sections.heading: The High Council
sections.body: The Empire is governed from the First City by a High Council of house leaders, headed by a Chancellor. The office is powerful, contested, and historically as likely to change hands by assassination or challenge as by succession — and the culture regards a successful challenge as a legitimate transfer rather than a coup, provided the forms were observed. The setting is candid that this system produces poor government. Chancellors spend their authority holding the Council together, houses obstruct policy for advantage, and the Empire's decline is repeatedly attributed by its own characters to leaders more interested in position than in the state. Honour as a public value coexists with a political culture that rewards its opposite. That gap is the Empire's central subject. Klingons who take the honour code seriously find themselves at odds with the institution that claims it, and the setting's most admired Klingon characters are almost always in that position.

sections.heading: Visiting
sections.body: Qo'noS receives outsiders, and the experience is not gentle. Federation visitors report heat, pressure, food that is alive and intended to be, drink that is genuinely dangerous, and a social register in which insult is a form of address and hesitation is read as weakness. Diplomatic missions there are considered demanding postings. Klingon hospitality is real and unmistakably its own. A guest is fed enormously, argued with vigorously, and defended absolutely against anyone else — and a visitor who joins the argument rather than enduring it is regarded far more favourably than one who is polite. The First City is ancient, monumental and built to intimidate, and the setting uses it as the Empire's self-portrait: a civilisation with a very long memory, considerable dignity, and no interest whatever in making anyone comfortable.

guides.title: Romulus and the Star Empire
guides.summary: The world the Vulcans left behind became: an empire built on secrecy, and a senate nobody quite trusts.

sections.heading: A Vulcan Offshoot
sections.body: Romulans and Vulcans share an origin. The Romulans descend from those who rejected the discipline of logic when it was adopted, left their homeworld, and settled two worlds elsewhere — Romulus and its companion. The setting reveals this comparatively late, and the revelation reframes both peoples: the Vulcans as a civilisation whose most famous virtue was a choice made against a real alternative, and the Romulans as what happens when that choice goes the other way. The result is a people with Vulcan physiology and none of Vulcan restraint — passionate, proud, deeply familial, and possessed of the same formidable intellect turned toward advantage rather than toward truth. Physically they are near-identical, which the setting exploits at every opportunity. The relationship between the two is not warm. Vulcans regard the Romulans as a road not taken; Romulans regard Vulcans as relatives who abandoned their nature and then lectured everyone about it.

sections.heading: Secrecy as Statecraft
sections.body: The Romulan Star Empire runs on concealment the way other powers run on force. Its worlds are closed, its intentions are stated obliquely, its fleets are cloaked, and its diplomacy assumes that every offer conceals a purpose — including its own. A Romulan negotiating in good faith is doing something their own culture would find slightly embarrassing. The internal instrument of this is the Tal Shiar, an intelligence service whose reach extends into the military, the Senate and private households, and which is feared by Romulans far more than by anyone outside. A state where the security service can remove a senator is a state where nobody's position is secure, and the setting's Romulan characters conduct themselves accordingly. The strategic consequence is that Romulan policy is hard to read from outside and frequently hard to read from inside. Long silences followed by sudden action are characteristic, and the Neutral Zone exists partly because nobody could establish what they wanted for long enough to negotiate about it.

sections.heading: The Senate
sections.body: Government is by a Senate headed by a Praetor, with the military as a distinct power centre and the intelligence service as a third. The setting's Romulan politics are consequently triangular, and its plots turn on which of the three is currently ascendant — a military commander who despises the Tal Shiar, a senator manoeuvring against the Praetor, an agent loyal to none of them. Romulan patriotism is genuine and is the thing the intrigue runs on. Officers who conspire do so for the Empire as they understand it, and the setting is careful to show that its Romulan antagonists are not cynics. They are people who believe the state is worth protecting from the people currently running it. That makes the Empire the setting's most usable political antagonist. It cannot be won over by an appeal to shared values, cannot be intimidated, and contains factions who would rather deal with the Federation than with each other — which is the only opening anyone ever gets.

sections.heading: The Worlds
sections.body: Romulus is described as green, temperate and beautiful, which is deliberately at odds with the reputation of the people on it. Its capital is monumental, its senate chamber theatrical, and its landscape is one of the few things Romulans discuss with visitors without calculation. The companion world shares the system and much of the culture, and the pairing is used to establish that the Empire is a genuine civilisation with a homeland rather than a fleet with a flag. Beyond them lies a large territory of subject and allied worlds administered with the same combination of competence and suspicion. Later material destroys the system entirely in a stellar catastrophe, scattering the survivors and shattering the Empire's coherence. Whatever a reader's view of that development, it changes the Romulans from a rival power into a diaspora, and everything written about them afterwards is written in that shadow.
